facts.statement: The study used developing retinal bipolar cells as a model to compare how cells move during different stages of tissue development.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Bipolar cells that are born before the photoreceptor layer forms move in a directed way that depends on microtubules.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Bipolar cells born later in development move in a more passive and less directed manner, which appears to be driven mainly by the movement of the surrounding tissue.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Blocking the movement of the whole tissue reduced the displacement of later-born cells, while preventing the formation of the photoreceptor layer caused later-born cells to move in a directed way.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Regardless of the movement strategy used, the bipolar cells ended up in the correct layer of the retina.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: The findings suggest that the surrounding tissue environment can influence how cells move, a principle that may apply to other developing tissues.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue
